title: What Cheer Gear You Actually Need (and What You Don't)
description: A first-season gear list for all-star cheer parents: what to buy before day one, what to wait on, what the gym must supply, and where the money gets wasted.
ogDescription: Buy this before day one. Wait on this. Never buy this. A first-season cheer gear list that isn't a wish list.
headline: What you *actually* need. And what you really don't.
sub: New cheer families routinely spend several hundred dollars before the first practice, most of it on things the gym was going to supply or the athlete will never use. Here is the honest starter list.

blocks.text: **Before you buy anything:** ask your gym for its required-items list in writing. Programs differ substantially on what must be purchased through the gym versus what families source themselves, and buying the wrong version of a required item is the most common avoidable gear expense in a first season.

There is a predictable pattern in a family's first all-star season. A kid makes a team in May. The parents, wanting to do this properly, go shopping. By the first practice they have spent several hundred dollars — and within a month roughly half of it turns out to have been unnecessary, duplicated by something the gym supplied, or the wrong specification entirely.

This is not because those parents were careless. It is because **the gym's required-items list usually arrives after the excitement does**, and because cheer retail is very good at presenting optional things as essential.
Here is what to buy, what to wait on, and what to skip.
Buy before the first practice
This is a genuinely short list. Four things.
Cheer shoes

The one purchase that affects performance and injury risk. **Check the gym's requirement first** — a meaningful number of programs specify a model and colorway, and some supply them directly. If your gym leaves it open, the attributes that matter are heel lock, sole thickness appropriate to the athlete's position, and a toe-box that fits her actual foot.
Budget **$60–$130**. For a first-season Level 1–2 athlete who will grow out of them, the budget end is genuinely fine. For a flyer at Level 3 or above, spend the money.
Practice wear (two sets, not five)

Fitted shorts and a fitted top or sports bra, in whatever the gym's practice dress code specifies. **Two sets is the correct starting number.** Cheer practice wear is sold in coordinated collections designed to make you buy six, and new families frequently do, then discover the gym requires a specific team set in month two.
Fitted matters for a real reason: coaches need to see body lines to correct technique, and loose clothing catches on hands during stunt transitions.
A bag that holds everything

Any durable backpack works for the first season. Cheer-branded bags run **$50–$90** and are genuinely well-shaped for the job, but a sturdy backpack your family already owns is not a compromise. Many gyms issue a team bag later anyway — **wait to see whether yours does before buying a branded one.**
A water bottle that survives a gym floor
Unglamorous, genuinely necessary. Practices run two to four hours in rooms that are frequently warm. Get something insulated with a lid that survives being dropped.
"Almost everything else on the cheer retail wall is either supplied by your gym, required in a specific version you don't own yet, or genuinely optional."
Wait until the gym tells you
These are all things families buy early and then re-buy in the correct version:

blocks.text: The rule of thumb: **if it appears on the competition floor, the gym probably specifies it.** Anything visible in a routine is part of a uniform standard, and buying your own version almost never works out.
Genuinely worth having (but not day one)

items: **A second pair of shoes** once the season is underway — practice shoes and competition shoes extends the life of both, and competition shoes stay clean
**Athletic tape and pre-wrap** — wrists and ankles, once the athlete is tumbling regularly
**A foam roller** — genuinely useful for an athlete training four-plus days a week, and cheaper than the recovery products marketed alongside it
**A small competition-day kit** — safety pins, bobby pins, clear nail polish, spare hair ties, snacks. Assemble it yourself; pre-made versions cost several times the parts
**A stunt mat or tumbling mat for home** — only if your athlete has somewhere safe to use it and a coach has said home practice is appropriate for her current skills

blocks.text: Skip these
Not because they are scams, but because the value-per-dollar is poor for a first-season family:

items: **Specialty "tumbling trainer" devices** — resistance straps, spotting belts, tumble tracks for home use. Skills develop under coach supervision on proper surfaces. These mostly develop bad habits.
**Full makeup kits before the gym specifies a look** — you will buy the specified palette anyway
**Multiple bow collections** — competition bows are team-specified; casual bows are decorative
**Branded everything** — the jacket, the blanket, the car decal, the phone case. None of it affects the season, all of it is priced at enthusiasm rather than cost.
**Anything sold at a competition venue** — venue retail is priced for impulse, and the same items are available cheaper from the same brands online

blocks.text: The one question that saves the most money
Before buying anything, ask the gym: **"What is the complete list of items I need to purchase, which of them must come through the gym, and when will each be invoiced?"**

That single question prevents nearly all first-season gear waste. It also tells you something useful about the program — a gym that can answer it immediately has thought about what it is asking families to spend. A gym that can't will be equally vague about the rest of your season's costs.
Buy the shoes, buy two sets of practice wear, get a decent bag and a water bottle, and wait. Everything else will announce itself.
